title: ADHD — 250 years in 57 events
_help: Merged from adhd-timeline.json (57 sourced steps: description | concept | tool | neuroscience | drug | diagnosis | genetics | theory | adoption) plus the Tier-1 closing wave. Each event lights the country where it happened (iso2); steps with iso2:null are narrative beats (map unchanged). `confidence` is high | medium | verify per adhd-timeline.json: medium = year/detail worth double-checking, verify = must be sourced before it goes on video. `sourceHint` is where to confirm, not a full citation. Ranges (1917–18, 1930s–50s) are folded into `year` because the player renders year only. Diffusion enrichment (alsoLit) lives in presentation_adhd_diffusion.json, keyed by step id — never hand-edit alsoLit here.

steps.label: Weikard: first written account
talkingPoints: Melchior Adam Weikard describes 'attentio volubilis' (inattention) in his medical text.
Not called ADHD, but the symptoms are recognizable.

steps.label: Crichton: 'mental restlessness'
talkingPoints: Scottish physician Alexander Crichton describes inability to attend with constancy.
Often cited as the first English-language description.

steps.label: Hoffmann: 'Fidgety Phil'
talkingPoints: Heinrich Hoffmann, a doctor, writes Struwwelpeter with Zappelphilipp, a child who cannot sit still.
Written 1844, first published 1845. A children's book, not a clinical paper.

steps.label: Amphetamine first synthesized
talkingPoints: Lazar Edeleanu synthesizes amphetamine in Berlin.
No medical use for decades.

steps.label: William James on attention
talkingPoints: Principles of Psychology frames attention as a core mental faculty and discusses its disorders.

steps.label: Still: 'defect of moral control'
talkingPoints: George Still's Goulstonian Lectures in The Lancet describe 43 children with impulsivity and poor attention.
Considered the first formal clinical description.

steps.label: Encephalitis epidemic
talkingPoints: Survivors, including children, show hyperactivity and behavior change.
Behavior problems are first linked to brain injury.

steps.label: First human EEG recorded
talkingPoints: Hans Berger records electrical brain activity from a human scalp.
Published in 1929. EEG later becomes the first brain tool used on ADHD.

steps.label: Alles rediscovers amphetamine
talkingPoints: Gordon Alles, searching for an ephedrine substitute, finds amphetamine's stimulant effect.

steps.label: 'Minimal brain damage' era
talkingPoints: Hyperactive children are assumed to have undetectable brain injury.
Term later softened to 'dysfunction'.
steps.sourceHint: Lange et al. 2010 history of ADHD

steps.label: Benzedrine inhaler goes on sale
talkingPoints: Smith, Kline & French markets amphetamine as a decongestant inhaler.
Tablets follow in 1935.

steps.label: Kramer & Pollnow: hyperkinetic disorder
talkingPoints: Franz Kramer and Hans Pollnow describe 'hyperkinetic disease' in children in Berlin.

steps.label: Bradley: Benzedrine calms children
talkingPoints: Charles Bradley gives Benzedrine to children at a Rhode Island home and sees better behavior and school performance.
First documented stimulant treatment of what becomes ADHD. Largely ignored for years.

steps.label: Methylphenidate synthesized
talkingPoints: Chemist Leandro Panizzon at Ciba creates it. Named Ritalin after his wife, Marguerite 'Rita'.
Patented 1954.

steps.label: Strauss: 'brain-injured child'
talkingPoints: Strauss and Lehtinen's book links hyperactivity to presumed brain damage, even without proof.
Sets up the 'minimal brain damage' era.

steps.label: FDA approves Ritalin
talkingPoints: Marketed from 1954 and approved by the FDA in 1955, at first for fatigue and other uses.
Use in children with hyperactivity grows through the 1960s.

steps.label: Dopamine shown to be a brain neurotransmitter
talkingPoints: Arvid Carlsson shows dopamine is a signaling molecule in the brain, not just a precursor to noradrenaline.
Wins the 2000 Nobel Prize.

steps.label: 'Hyperkinetic impulse disorder' coined
talkingPoints: Maurice Laufer and colleagues name a behavioral syndrome instead of a brain injury.

steps.label: Dopamine deficit found in Parkinson's
talkingPoints: Oleh Hornykiewicz shows dopamine is depleted in Parkinson's brains.
Proves dopamine matters for behavior and movement.

steps.label: 'Minimal brain dysfunction'
talkingPoints: Clements and Peters formalize MBD with a long symptom list.
Too vague to be useful, which drives later reform.

steps.label: DSM-II: 'Hyperkinetic reaction of childhood'
talkingPoints: First official US diagnosis. Assumed to fade by adolescence.

steps.label: Douglas: attention, not activity, is the core problem
talkingPoints: Virginia Douglas in Montreal argues sustained attention and impulse control matter more than hyperactivity.

steps.label: Feingold diet
talkingPoints: Ben Feingold claims food additives cause hyperactivity.
Studies since have not supported it as a general cause.

steps.label: MRI imaging invented
talkingPoints: Paul Lauterbur produces the first MR image.
Peter Mansfield in the UK develops fast imaging. They share the 2003 Nobel Prize.

steps.label: First dopamine model of hyperactivity
talkingPoints: Shaywitz and colleagues damage dopamine neurons in rat pups and get hyperactivity that stimulants reduce.

steps.label: First human MRI scans
talkingPoints: Whole-body human scans appear in 1977, with Damadian's team in the US and Mansfield's fast imaging in the UK around the same time.

steps.label: DSM-III: ADD
talkingPoints: Renamed 'attention deficit disorder', with or without hyperactivity. Attention moves to the center.

steps.label: DSM-III-R: ADHD
talkingPoints: The name becomes ADHD, with one combined symptom list.

steps.label: BOLD contrast discovered
talkingPoints: Seiji Ogawa at Bell Labs shows MRI can detect blood oxygen changes, the basis of fMRI.

steps.label: PET: lower frontal metabolism in ADHD adults
talkingPoints: Zametkin at NIMH finds reduced brain glucose metabolism in parents of ADHD children.

steps.label: First human fMRI
talkingPoints: Teams at Massachusetts General Hospital, Minnesota and Wisconsin independently publish the first human functional MRI studies.

steps.label: Hunter vs. farmer theory
talkingPoints: Thom Hartmann proposes ADHD people are 'hunters in a farmer's world'.
A popular idea, not an established scientific finding. Evolutionary hypotheses are still debated.

steps.label: DSM-IV: three subtypes
talkingPoints: Inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive and combined presentations.

steps.label: Adult ADHD enters public awareness
talkingPoints: Hallowell and Ratey's 'Driven to Distraction' brings adult ADHD to a mass audience.

steps.label: Dopamine transporter gene linked to ADHD
talkingPoints: Cook et al. report an association with DAT1, the target of methylphenidate.
steps.sourceHint: Cook et al. 1995, Am J Hum Genet

steps.label: Adderall approved for ADHD
talkingPoints: Mixed amphetamine salts become a first-line option.

steps.label: Structural MRI: smaller brain regions in ADHD
talkingPoints: Castellanos finds smaller volumes in frontal and basal ganglia regions in boys with ADHD.
steps.sourceHint: Castellanos et al. 1996, Arch Gen Psychiatry

steps.label: DRD4 gene linked to ADHD
talkingPoints: LaHoste et al. link the DRD4 7-repeat allele to ADHD, fueling the evolutionary 'novelty-seeking' story.
Effect sizes are small.

steps.label: Methylphenidate shown to block dopamine transporter in humans
talkingPoints: Volkow's PET work shows therapeutic doses occupy most DAT sites and raise dopamine levels.
steps.sourceHint: Volkow et al. 1998, Am J Psychiatry; 2001

steps.label: First fMRI studies of ADHD
talkingPoints: Bush (US) and Rubia (UK) report underactive frontal and cingulate regions during attention tasks.
steps.sourceHint: Bush et al. 1999; Rubia et al. 1999

steps.label: NIMH MTA study
talkingPoints: Largest ADHD treatment trial. Careful medication management beat behavioral therapy alone at 14 months.

steps.label: Concerta: once-daily extended release
talkingPoints: Extended-release methylphenidate means no school-day dosing. Adderall XR and others follow in 2001.

steps.label: Atomoxetine (Strattera): first non-stimulant
talkingPoints: Eli Lilly's noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor gets FDA approval for ADHD in 2002.
Non-controlled, with slower onset than stimulants.

steps.label: Atomoxetine reaches Europe
talkingPoints: Launched in the UK and other European markets around 2004.
steps.sourceHint: EMA / MHRA; mutual recognition procedure dates

steps.label: ADHD heritability about 75%
talkingPoints: Meta-analyses of twin studies put heritability around 0.76, among the highest for psychiatric conditions.

steps.label: Japan approves Concerta for ADHD
talkingPoints: Japan's approach to stimulants stays tightly regulated. Atomoxetine follows in 2009.

steps.label: Delayed cortical maturation
talkingPoints: NIMH finds the cortex thickens later in ADHD, by about three years, rather than being absent.

steps.label: Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine)
talkingPoints: A prodrug of dextroamphetamine, designed to lower abuse potential.

steps.label: Nomads and DRD4: evolutionary evidence
talkingPoints: Among Ariaal people in Kenya, 7-repeat carriers did better as nomads, a data point for the hunter-gatherer idea.
One study, so treat it as suggestive.
steps.sourceHint: Eisenberg et al. 2008, BMC Evol Biol

steps.label: NICE issues first UK ADHD guideline
talkingPoints: Sets out treatment pathways for children and adults. Updated in 2018.

steps.label: Japan approves atomoxetine
talkingPoints: A non-stimulant option arrives where stimulant access is limited.

steps.label: Dopamine reward pathway deficits in ADHD adults
talkingPoints: Volkow's PET study finds lower dopamine receptor and transporter availability linked to motivation.

steps.label: DSM-5: adult ADHD recognized
talkingPoints: Onset by age 12 instead of 7, with symptom criteria adjusted for adults.

steps.label: FDA clears first EEG-based ADHD aid
talkingPoints: The NEBA system uses the theta/beta ratio as a diagnostic aid. It cannot diagnose alone, and the evidence is debated.

steps.label: Viloxazine (Qelbree) approved
talkingPoints: Another non-stimulant, joining atomoxetine, guanfacine and clonidine.

steps.label: International consensus statement
talkingPoints: The World Federation of ADHD publishes 208 evidence-based conclusions confirming ADHD as a valid, treatable condition.
steps.sourceHint: Faraone et al. 2021, Neurosci Biobehav Rev

steps.label: Adderall shortage
talkingPoints: Supply problems follow rising diagnoses and manufacturing limits, and continue for years.

steps.label: Today: stimulant-first access in 41 countries
talkingPoints: The story so far ends here: 41 countries with amphetamine-class access lit at once. This claims the present, from the tier dataset — not a dated history. The rest of the map is still grey.
